segments.text: Episode seventy-four. Next stop... cosmic rays.
In nineteen twelve, scientist Victor Hess took a balloon flight more than five kilometers high, carrying instruments to measure radiation.
segments.headline: A balloon flight, 1912

segments.text: He expected radiation to fade as he rose away from the ground. Instead, it got stronger. It was coming from space.
segments.headline: Radiation from space

segments.text: He had discovered cosmic rays, and won the Nobel Prize for it.
Cosmic rays are mostly protons and atomic nuclei, racing through space at nearly the speed of light.
segments.headline: Particles at light speed

segments.text: When they hit our atmosphere, they shatter into showers of particles. Some are passing through you right now.
segments.headline: Particle showers

segments.text: In nineteen ninety-one, a detector in Utah caught the most energetic particle ever seen. Scientists called it the Oh-My-God particle.
segments.headline: The Oh-My-God particle

segments.text: A single proton carried about the energy of a baseball thrown fast. Millions of times more than our best particle colliders.
Where do these monsters come from? Exploding stars, black holes, colliding galaxies? Nobody knows for sure.
segments.headline: Where from? Unknown

segments.text: Tomorrow, ghost particles. Trillions are flying through your body this second. Next stop: neutrinos. Follow, so you don't miss episode seventy-five.
